content.thinking:
I'm planning out the capybara's proportions and whimsical design — a chubby barrel-shaped body with a blocky head, tiny ears, small eyes, and a small bird perched on top — then sketching the skeleton structure starting from the hips as the root joint.

I'm working through the joint hierarchy: spine chain up through the neck, head, and jaw, four legs, a tail stub, ear joints, and separate bird joints parented to the head for the perched bird, possibly with hinge joints for wings. I want to keep the fur approach simple using paint techniques like mottle, countershade, and grain rather than a full toon kit, and I'm mapping out spine coordinates using a catmull curve from rump to chest while deciding how to structure the chain so the joint names align properly with the spans.

Now I'm continuing the chain upward: a neck chain running from the spine's last joint to the head base, followed by a head joint positioned further forward and angled slightly downward since the head needs to extend out toward the nose like a capybara's long skull.

For the head itself, I'm lofting from the skull base out to a blunt, tall snout, then adding details — a dark nose pad, nostrils, lips, small high-set eyes, rounded ears near the back of the skull, and a jaw joint positioned to aim toward the nose for a separate lower jaw piece.

For the legs, I'm defining the front limb using a shoulder-to-foot target with segment lengths that sum close to the actual distance, working out the bend direction for a natural joint.

For naming, I'm deciding that positive x corresponds to the left side since world +X points left, so I'll append "L" for that side and derive the opposite accordingly, parenting front legs to the spine and rear legs to the hips. For the hind legs I'm setting similar hip-to-foot targets with two roughly equal-length segments.

Checking the knee bend direction and foot placement so the tip joint sits near ground level, then sweeping the leg chain with tapering radii so the rounded cap barely dips below the ground plane, which should still be negligible relative to the body height. I'm adjusting the foot's final joint height and radius so the sweep's rounded bottom lands close to y=0 without poking through noticeably.

For the toes, I'll add three small dark-brown spheres angled forward near the ground, sized so they just graze the floor without sinking too far.

For the body, I'm working out how to loft it along a bone chain spanning from the hips through the spine to the neck, since the body needs to stretch from the rump near the tail to the base of the head, and the hips need to be included as part of that chain rather than treated as an isolated joint.

Now I'm laying out the width and height stations for the barrel-shaped torso, matching capybara proportions, and setting the vertical center height above where the legs will attach to the floor.

Adjusting the spine and neck chain coordinates and heights...

Still working out proportions...

For the coat, I'm layering a countershaded mottle pattern using warm brownish-orange tones, darker on top and lighter on the belly. I'll add sparse fur tufts scattered across the body using a simple triangular svg shape with some randomized spacing and lean, keeping the texture modest rather than overly dense.

For the white tuft texture, I realize fill it as white/grey so it tints naturally with the coat color beneath. Then I'm adding a few thin dark whisker rods on the muzzle, and sculpting the nose pad as a small dark flattened sphere near the top of the snout with two tiny darker nostril spheres embedded in it.

Now placing the eyes as small dark spheres with tiny white highlight dots, positioned just outside the head loft width so they read clearly. I'm adding subtle brow and cheek-blush details using small flattened spheres in coat and pinkish tones, then shaping the ears as small rounded, scaled spheres set near the top sides of the head.

I'm working through the jaw and mouth structure now, considering whether to render the lower jaw as a visible lip band using a frustum shape, since the head loft already encloses that region and I want the mouth to read clearly without clipping.

Adding small cream incisor boxes near the mouth for cute buck teeth, then setting up the jaw joint parented to the head. Since capybaras barely have tails, I'm adding just a tiny nub joint behind the hips for a small rump bump.

Now I'm placing a whimsical little bird perched on the head: a rounded body sphere sunk slightly into the head's crown, with a small head sphere and beak positioned above it, sized and colored like a playful blue-yellow songbird.

Adding the finer bird details - tiny dark eyes, small flattened wing shapes on each side, a flat tapered tail spike extending backward, orange rod feet tucked into the head, and a little crest tuft of three small spikes on top of its head.

I could add a small yuzu fruit detail near the bird as a whimsical nod to capybara stories, maybe a tiny orange sphere placed near its position, though I'm wary of overcrowding the head. For the body, the dorsal stripe and countershading can just be handled through the coat paint gradient rather than separate geometry.

Now I'm working out the paint logic for the head and legs—using darker sector colors on the body, a gradient blending the coat tone into a lighter muzzle shade, and darker gradients for the legs to ground the color scheme naturally across the model.

For fur, I'm scattering tuft cards over the body's sweep surface, filtering out the underside, sizing and bending each tuft for a natural flow, and confirming the coat paint applies correctly at the root level for countershading.

I'm wiring up the loft call with stations bound to the hips-spine-neck bone chain, checking that the body stations extend properly into the neck and head region, then setting up the neck sweep with its own radius profile along the chain path.

Now I'm defining the head loft as a rigid piece parented to the head joint, then sketching out the full joint hierarchy (spine, neck, head, jaw, ears, shoulders, legs, tail) and placing the ear joints as hinges parented to the head at specific offsets and directions.

For legs, I'm building front limb chains for both sides using a shared geometry function, checking segment distances stay within rig limits, and setting the elbow bend direction backward for front legs (forward for hind legs), then creating the chain parented to the appropriate spine joint with named shoulder/elbow/hand segments.

Then I'm sweeping a tapered tube along each leg chain with thicker radius near the shoulder, and adding small toe spheres offset along the foot at the chain's tip position.

Now I'm setting up the hind legs with hip, knee, and foot joints scaled by side, checking the bend distances fit within the limb lengths, and sweeping thicker radii for the hind leg segments.

I'm thinking about adding a haunch bulge for the hind hip using a scaled ellipsoid, and planning a reusable `ball` helper for sphere-based body parts with bone attachment, position, and scale options.

Now I'm working out whiskers as thin rods sweeping outward from the snout, then detailing the eyes as small dark spheres with tiny white highlight spheres positioned relative to head width.

Now I'm sketching helper functions for the texture, keeping the flat color count under the limit since paints don't count toward it. I'm defining a small tuft SVG path and figuring out how it gets tinted by the part's color, then moving to crest/feather spikes using a spike helper with base, direction, length, and radius parameters.

Still placing bird parts...

Still placing small feet and toe spikes...

Now adding two yuzu fruit balls on the head with a small flattened green leaf on top, positioning them so they rest naturally at the top of the head sphere. I'm also checking that the bird body sinks slightly into the head surface so it looks seated rather than floating.

Next I'm placing the ears near the top edges of the head, scaling them thin and tilting them with a slight rotation for a natural angle, plus adding small pinkish inner-ear shapes offset toward the front.

Now I'm double-checking the imports to avoid unused-variable type errors, confirming the limb function signature takes root, target, lengths, and bend arrays, and verifying the loft station points match the expected vector type before adding a surface scatter pass for texture detail.

Checking the sweep sector tuples and paint definitions for the body's countershading and dorsal mottle pattern, then adding the hip joint as part of the spine chain.

I'm working through the joint hierarchy: the spine chain from hips to three spine joints, the neck chain to two neck joints, then head and jaw joints with parent-child relationships and aim targets. Finally I'm placing a small tail nub ball joint at the tail root with a dark color and scaled-down dimensions.

Checking that everything stays above the floor - toes, legs, and body bottom all clear zero. Now I'm setting up the TypeScript helper functions, importing the Joint type from the skeleton module to type the bone parameters correctly, then defining the ball/part helpers inside the build function before writing the final metadata (name, description, whimsical style) and committing the code.
